strengths: NCI offers a useful, simple post-hoc detector combining centered feature alignment with classifier weights and feature magnitude. Its additional scoring cost is O(P), without nearest-neighbor search or subspace decomposition. Table 1b reports latency comparable to MSP: 0.54 versus 0.53 ms on CIFAR-10 and 6.84 versus 6.85 ms on ImageNet.

Evaluation covers CIFAR-10, CIFAR-100, ImageNet, and four architecture families, including near- and far-OOD datasets. There are meaningful improvements: Table 2 reports Swin FPR95 of 65.83 versus 75.70 for KNN, and Table 9 reports strong DenseNet AUROCs of 94.49 and 83.26. This breadth supports practical value without requiring universal benchmark leadership.

The ablations provide useful evidence for the score components. Adding the norm term improves ImageNet SSB-hard AUROC from 66.81 to 73.90 and iNaturalist from 92.67 to 96.95. Table 7 consistently favors pScore over cosine similarity and the proposed Euclidean alternative.
The score is clearly specified, and checkpoint references, a small hyperparameter grid, implementation details, and a code link provide a reasonable starting point for reproduction.
weaknesses: The practical merits are balanced by substantive problems in the central explanation. Sections 3.1–3.2 claim that forming an ETF necessitates sufficiently large feature norms. ETF geometry is invariant to uniform positive scaling, so it does not establish this expansion or an ID/OOD norm ordering. Moreover, NC2 concerns centered features, whereas the filter uses the uncentered norm. The filter has empirical support, but its claimed explanation through neural collapse is not established.

Theorem 3.1 overstates what its proof establishes. Equation 4 concerns convergence after normalization by the class-mean norm; obtaining the unnormalized convergence in Equation 2 requires additional bounds or convergence-rate assumptions. Also, the absolute covariance collapse assumed in NC1 differs from the relative covariance statistic illustrated in supplementary Figure 7. A directional alignment statement would better match the argument.

Several numerical summaries do not match their constituent results. In Table 2, NCI's five ViT AUROCs average 94.84, whereas the reported AVG is 93.64. In Table 9, Energy's CIFAR-100 FPR95 values average 64.47, whereas 94.47 is reported. These inconsistencies complicate verification of the headline aggregate-performance claims, although correcting them need not eliminate NCI's advantages.

The architectural comparison omits the closest neural-collapse-based competitor, NECO, from Table 2 and consequently Table 3. This matters because robustness across architectures is a principal contribution. Algorithmically, Equation 6 simplifies to w_c^T(h−μ_G)/||h−μ_G||₂, so the novelty is principally an efficient combination of established alignment and magnitude cues. The manuscript does not sufficiently establish its architectural advantage over the closest related approach.

Mechanistic validation is narrower than the detection evaluation: Figures 1–2 analyze CIFAR-10/SVHN, while Appendix 13 reproduces prior neural-collapse results rather than measurements on the evaluated checkpoints. Reproducibility also has smaller gaps, including the Gaussian validation-set size and selection criterion, DenseNet filtering strengths, and timing protocol. Table 5 establishes only local sensitivity around one setting on one model.
